An empire is not the empire of today where you can exert authority everywhere. Empire at this time is mainly controlling certain choke points of trade, with everyone else just going along because it benefits them. An empire is more like a loose confederation as opposed to a nation state. The Assyrian Empire and the Neo-Assyrian Empire are examples of such empires that constantly change over time.

History changes when a man named Cyrus the Great emerges. Cyrus the Great is the founder of something called the Persian Academic Empire.

Last class, we discussed Zoroastrianism, which is really the first great world religion because it provides a simple but powerful model of how the world works. Rationalism is powerful because it encourages everyone to be their best and seek Asha, where for most people, Asha means don't ever lie. When you run an empire, you need soldiers, generals, and administrators. If people are honest and moral, you can expand quickly.

Cyrus the Great is also known for his mercy and generosity. When he conquers a place, he identifies the best people, maybe even the king himself, and makes them advisers to his regime. He's known for his tolerance and openness. The Babylonian Empire basically surrendered to him without a fight because of elite overproduction—there was a conflict between upper and lower nobility who invited Cyrus to resolve their conflicts.

Cyrus the Great built the first world empire. This is how the fall of Babylon unfolded: they invited him in to resolve their inner conflicts. There's a tomb of Cyrus the Great still in Iran today, though it's said that when Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire and discovered Cyrus' tomb was in bad repair, he ordered for it to be properly maintained. That story is probably false but shows respect for Cyrus at that time.

The Persian Empire encompasses most of West Asia, from Iran all the way to Mesopotamia, Anatolia, parts of Greece, Egypt, and Libya. They were able to manage this vast area through innovations in religion and administration.

Traditional ways of ruling empires include controlling trade routes and access, using fear and conquest, or taking hostages. The Persians did well with effective administration, meritocracy, and communication networks like roads and postal systems.
